findings.failure_scenario: A company entity scores >= settings.signal_scan_auto_threshold (0.60, app/config.py:91-93) during process_entity_scorer_job, which auto-enqueues a signal_scan job (app/services/agent_pipeline.py:670-677, enqueue_signal_scan). When run_agent_job_cycle later claims that job, process_signal_scan_job (app/services/signal_engine.py:389-462) runs up to len(signals)/batch_size sequential LLM calls, each with timeout_seconds=480 (line 445); batch_size defaults to 25 (app/config.py:97) and a full scan covers 200 signals (module docstring, signal_engine.py:3-4) => up to 8 sequential batches, each individually budgeted up to 480s (worst case 3840s for one job). All of this happens inside the SAME AsyncSession opened once at the top of run_agent_job_cycle (agent_pipeline.py:724) and held for the entire cycle. Meanwhile app/tasks/agent_jobs.py:14 wraps the WHOLE cycle in `asyncio.wait_for(run_agent_job_cycle(limit=limit), timeout=900)` with zero surrounding try/except in that file. If the cycle is still inside process_signal_scan_job's batch loop (or anywhere else) when the 900s budget expires, asyncio.wait_for cancels the underlying coroutine: a real asyncio.CancelledError is raised at whatever await point the cycle is suspended on. Since Python 3.8, CancelledError subclasses BaseException, not Exception, so it is NOT caught by the per-job `except Exception as error:` at agent_pipeline.py:757 (the already-fixed motivating-bug handler) -- it propagates straight through, unrolled-back for that job, past run_agent_job_cycle, gets turned into asyncio.TimeoutError by wait_for at the agent_jobs.py:14 call site, and then propagates uncaught out of run_agent_jobs() (no try/except anywhere in app/tasks/agent_jobs.py) and out of asyncio.run() in __main__. `python -m app.tasks.agent_jobs` exits non-zero; entrypoint.sh's `set -e` (line 2) propagates that to the container exit code; Railway reports 'Deploy Crashed'. The in-flight job is left with status='running' and a live lease (claimed at agent_pipeline.py:739-748 and committed at line 731 before the loop) until claim_pending_jobs' 45-minute stale-lease reclaim (app/services/job_queue.py:136,154) picks it back up -- i.e. it is not lost, but it is stuck and unreported for up to 45 minutes, and every other job still queued in that cycle's batch of up to `limit` (default 25) never gets a turn.
findings.reachability_evidence: Mechanism traced exhaustively via literal citations above (app/tasks/agent_jobs.py:14, app/services/agent_pipeline.py:724,739-748,757, app/services/signal_engine.py:389-456, app/config.py:91-97). Whether it fires on a *typical* production run depends on real LLM batch latency, which is not observable from the corpus (no logs/metrics available here) -- but the configured ceiling (up to 8 batches x 480s = 3840s against a 900s budget) makes this reachable well before any pathological edge case, since even 2 batches at close to the per-batch timeout already exceeds the 900s budget.

findings.symbol: trigger_nightly_scan (and 5 sibling handlers: trigger_morning_digest:232, trigger_notion_sync:242, trigger_notion_control_plane:252, trigger_agent_jobs:262, trigger_cadence_scan:272)
findings.failure_scenario: Each of these 6 HTTP endpoints is a parallel, manually-triggerable invocation path for the same 6 task functions that Railway's TASK_MODE crons run. They fire the task with a bare `asyncio.create_task(...)`: no variable holds the returned Task, no `await`, no `.add_done_callback`, no exception handler is attached. If the underlying coroutine raises (any of the causes covered by B-01/B-05/B-06/B-07, or an ordinary llm/db_error/external failure that its own internal except-and-reraise lets through, e.g. app/tasks/nightly_scan.py:21-23), CPython's default asyncio exception handler prints 'Task exception was never retrieved' plus a traceback to stderr and moves on -- the FastAPI/uvicorn process does NOT crash (fire-and-forget task exceptions do not propagate to the event loop or terminate it), so Railway's crash-based alerting never fires either. The HTTP caller already received `{"status": "accepted"}` before the task even started running, so they have no way to learn it failed. This is the mirror image of B-01/B-08: instead of an over-loud crash, the failure is completely silent -- no crash, no alert, no error surfaced to the caller, only a stderr line that nothing is known to read.
findings.reachability_evidence: Cause-agnostic: any exception the six wrapped task functions can raise (LLM, DB, network, or a re-raised timeout per B-05/06/07) triggers this failure mode identically. Reachable whenever /tasks/* is called with a valid X-Cron-Secret (app/api/deps.py:17-22) -- there is no code-level restriction limiting this to non-production use.

open_questions.topic: Contract shape: the given subclass taxonomy does not cover every defect shape found
open_questions.description: The requested subclass enum is no_rollback | orm_read_in_handler | escapes_to_process_exit | batch_lost_on_item_failure | session_lifecycle. Three of the findings above (B-01's CancelledError-vs-Exception type mismatch, B-04's fire-and-forget asyncio.create_task whose exception is never retrieved by anyone, and B-05/B-06/B-07's caught-but-swallowed asyncio.TimeoutError that turns a real failure into a false process-success) do not map cleanly onto any of the five: B-01 involves no database session at all (it is a pure exception-type gap between what asyncio.wait_for's cancellation raises and what the handler catches); B-04 is the inverse of escapes_to_process_exit (the exception explicitly does NOT escape to anywhere observable -- it is dropped); B-05/06/07 are the inverse of batch_lost_on_item_failure (nothing is lost from a batch, the whole run is abandoned but reported as a success). I mapped each to the closest existing label and described the actual mechanism in failure_scenario, but a revised taxonomy for this corpus would likely want two more subclasses: unretrieved_task_exception and swallowed_timeout_masks_success.
open_questions.evidence: See findings B-01, B-04, B-05, B-06, B-07 above for the literal mechanism each represents.

open_questions.topic: What should happen when a task entrypoint's asyncio.wait_for budget is exceeded?
open_questions.description: The 6 TASK_MODE entrypoints implement 3 different behaviors for structurally the same situation (an outer wait_for around the task's main work): (1) agent_jobs.py and cadence_scan.py have no try/except at all, so ANY exception -- a genuine timeout, an internal bug, a DB outage -- crashes the process and pages via Railway's Deploy Crashed alert. (2) morning_digest.py, nightly_scan.py, and notion_export.py catch asyncio.TimeoutError specifically and swallow it (log only, no raise), so a timeout is reported as success, while every OTHER exception type is logged and re-raised (crashes). (3) notion_control_plane.py has no asyncio.wait_for at all -- no outer runtime budget, bounded only by the sum of its internal per-call httpx timeouts (30s each) and however many Sources/API calls it loops through.
options: A: standardize on 'crash and alert' for every timeout (match agent_jobs.py/cadence_scan.py's current behavior for the other 4 tasks; requires removing the swallow-and-log-only branches in morning_digest.py/nightly_scan.py/notion_export.py).

B: standardize on 'log and report a distinguishable non-success' for every timeout across all 6 tasks (requires adding try/except + wait_for to agent_jobs.py, cadence_scan.py, and notion_control_plane.py, and giving every task a way to signal 'ran but did not finish' distinct from both full success and a hard crash -- e.g. a nonzero-but-not-traceback exit code, or a row written to a task-run log).
open_questions.evidence: app/tasks/agent_jobs.py:12-15, app/tasks/cadence_scan.py:13-22, app/tasks/morning_digest.py:15-25, app/tasks/nightly_scan.py:16-23, app/tasks/notion_export.py:15-23, app/tasks/notion_control_plane.py:16-51 (no wait_for present).

open_questions.topic: Should the Notion-writing sync loops commit per item?
open_questions.description: sync_findings_to_ocean, sync_source_registry_to_notion, and sync_watch_targets_to_notion each perform a real, non-idempotent Notion write (create_page/update_page) per item inside a loop, then commit once after the whole loop. Because Notion page creation is not idempotent and the query that selects 'work to do' is based on notion_page_id IS NULL, a mid-loop failure causes the next run to re-create pages that were already successfully created on the previous, failed run (B-02, B-03).
options: A: commit after each successfully-synced item (weaker atomicity per call, but no duplicate Notion pages on partial failure).

B: keep one commit per call, but make Notion writes idempotent some other way (e.g. look up by a stable external key before creating, or store a client-generated idempotency key Notion can dedupe on, if the Notion API supports one).
C: leave as-is if duplicate Notion pages on rare partial failure are considered an acceptable, manually-cleaned-up cost.

open_questions.topic: Are the /tasks/* HTTP trigger endpoints meant to be a production-parallel invocation path?
open_questions.description: app/api/routes.py:216-273 exposes the same 6 tasks Railway's TASK_MODE crons run, behind only a shared X-Cron-Secret header, invoked via a fire-and-forget asyncio.create_task with no result tracking (B-04). Failures via this path are invisible to both the HTTP caller and to any alerting, which is a materially weaker guarantee than the TASK_MODE cron path.
options: A: intended as a permanent manual-ops convenience -- if so, it needs its own failure-observability (e.g. persisted task-run records, or return a pollable status) since it currently has none.
B: intended only for local/staging testing and should not be reachable in production, or should be logged/alerted distinctly from a normal request.
C: not actually needed given TASK_MODE already covers scheduling -- candidate for removal.
